concepts.title: Classification of Carbohydrates
concepts.definition: Sugars are ranked by how many single-sugar units they carry: monosaccharides are the indivisible simple sugars fitting Cn(H2O)n, oligosaccharides join two to ten units through glycosidic bonds, and polysaccharides chain together more than ten; sugars conjugated to proteins or lipids form glycoproteins, proteoglycans and glycolipids.
concepts.key_idea: Count the building blocks to name the class, and note which partner the sugar carries when it decorates another macromolecule.
question_patterns: describe the classification of carbohydrates into monosaccharides oligosaccharides and polysaccharides
give the general formula of a monosaccharide and name one aldose and one ketose hexose
which class of carbohydrate do maltose lactose and sucrose belong to - justify
differentiate a glycoprotein from a proteoglycan and from a glycolipid
name the two monosaccharides obtained when sucrose is hydrolysed by boiling with dilute acid
list the triose tetrose pentose and hexose members of the monosaccharide table

solution_steps.explain: One unit is a monosaccharide, two to ten make an oligosaccharide, more than ten a polysaccharide.
Aldoses carry a free aldehyde group, ketoses a ketone group; both also bear hydroxyl groups.
Protein-dominant conjugates are glycoproteins, carbohydrate-dominant ones proteoglycans, lipid conjugates glycolipids.

worked_examples.q: Sugar chains of more than ten units joined by glycosidic bonds are called what?

concepts.title: Stereoisomers, Anomers and Epimers of Sugars
concepts.definition: Every asymmetric carbon doubles the possible spatial forms of a sugar, so n chiral centres allow 2 raised to n stereoisomers; glucose alone thus has sixteen, ring closure creates alpha and beta anomers that interconvert by mutarotation, and sugars differing at a single carbon such as mannose at C-2 or galactose at C-4 are epimers.
concepts.key_idea: Two to the power of chiral centres counts all stereoisomers; one differing carbon makes epimers, one differing anomeric carbon makes anomers.
question_patterns: glucose contains four chiral centres - how many stereoisomers does that allow
why does glyceraldehyde give only two stereoisomers while glucose gives sixteen
define anomers and explain what happens during mutarotation of glucose in water
name the two most important epimers of glucose and the carbon atom at which each differs
what decides whether a sugar belongs to the D or the L series
why are almost all sugars of biological systems the D form

solution_steps.explain: Locate carbons bonded to four different groups; glyceraldehyde has one, glucose four.
Each chiral centre doubles the number of spatial arrangements.

worked_examples.q: How many stereoisomers do glucose's four chiral centres allow?

concepts.title: Storage and Structural Polysaccharides
concepts.definition: Long sugar chains either bank energy or build bodies: starch in plants blends about 15-20 percent unbranched amylose with the rest being branched amylopectin, glycogen serves the same fuel role in animals, while cellulose and chitin supply load-bearing walls and exoskeletons; humans cannot digest cellulose for lack of cellulase, though cattle gut microbes can.
concepts.key_idea: Subtract the amylose fraction from 100 to price the branched amylopectin fraction of starch.
question_patterns: starch contains 15 to 20 percent amylose - what percent range does amylopectin occupy
differentiate amylose from amylopectin with reference to branching and linkage type
why can cattle digest cellulose while humans cannot
which polysaccharide turns blue with iodine and which gives a dull reddish brown shade
name the homopolysaccharide that stiffens the insect exoskeleton and its repeating unit
how does lysozyme in tears kill bacteria - answer with the bond it hydrolyses in peptidoglycan
where do branch points occur in amylopectin and which linkage joins them

solution_steps.explain: Amylose makes up 15-20 percent of natural starch.
The remaining starch fraction is branched amylopectin.

worked_examples.q: Starch's unbranched component is called what: amylose or amylopectin?

concepts.title: Fatty Acid Notation and Unsaturation
concepts.definition: Fatty chains are written carbon-count colon double-bond-count, with delta superscripts fixing where the unsaturation falls, so 18:2 (delta 9,12) is linoleic acid; being assembled from two-carbon pieces, natural chains carry even carbon totals, and each double bond removes two hydrogens from the saturated formula.
concepts.key_idea: Decode the notation to read chain length and unsaturation; every double bond costs two hydrogens.
question_patterns: expand the notation 18:2 (delta 9,12) - name the acid and locate its double bonds
a fatty acid has 18 carbons and two double bonds - how many hydrogen atoms does its acyclic formula hold
why do naturally occurring fatty acids always contain an even number of carbon atoms
differentiate monounsaturated from polyunsaturated fatty acids with one named example of each
write the shorthand symbols of palmitic oleic and arachidonic acids
numbering from the carboxyl carbon which carbons carry the double bonds in linolenic acid

solution_steps.explain: An acyclic saturated chain of n carbons carries 2n hydrogens.
Each unsaturation replaces two C-H pairs with a C=C link.

worked_examples.q: In fatty acid notation 18:2, what does the 2 count: double bonds or carbons?

concepts.title: Lipid Classes from Triacylglycerol to Steroids
concepts.definition: Simple lipids are plain fatty-acid esters - triacylglycerols bank energy in adipose tissue and waxes coat surfaces - while compound lipids add extra groups, as in amphipathic phospholipids whose two tails and phosphate head build membranes, and steroids whose four fused rings include cholesterol, the precursor of steroid hormones.
concepts.key_idea: Ester linkages join fatty chains to glycerol; amphipathic heads-and-tails make membranes, fused rings make steroids.
question_patterns: why are membrane lipids called amphipathic - explain using the phospholipid structure
differentiate simple lipids from compound lipids with two examples of each
what distinguishes a sphingolipid backbone from a glycerophospholipid backbone
which bond joins fatty acids to glycerol in a triacylglycerol
why is cholesterol called the precursor of steroid hormones and where is it synthesised
what is a micelle and when do phospholipids form one
which lipid stores energy in adipose tissue and which forms the protective coating on tropical leaves

solution_steps.explain: Esters of fatty acids with alcohols and nothing else are simple lipids; added groups make them compound lipids.
Glycerol backs glycerophospholipids; a sphingoid base backs sphingolipids joined by amide linkage.
Four fused rings identify steroids such as cholesterol, phytosterols and ergosterol.

worked_examples.q: Which lipid class banks energy in adipose tissue: triacylglycerol or cholesterol?

concepts.title: Amino Acids and the Zwitterion
concepts.definition: Each of the twenty standard amino acids is a central alpha carbon holding a carboxyl group, an amino group, a hydrogen and a variable side chain; at physiological pH proton transfer leaves the molecule dipolar - a zwitterion - and only L forms enter proteins.
concepts.key_idea: Only the R group changes across the twenty standards; ionised plus and minus poles make the zwitterion.
question_patterns: what is a zwitterion - draw its structure for glycine
name the four groups attached to the alpha carbon of an amino acid
classify the twenty standard amino acids on the basis of their R groups
which amino acid has the simplest side chain and which has a methyl side chain
differentiate non-standard amino acids from non-protein amino acids with examples
why do only L isomers of amino acids occur in proteins
how are the carbons of lysine numbered using Greek letters

solution_steps.explain: Central carbon with COOH, NH2, H and R group; the alpha carbon of most amino acids is asymmetric.
The proton shifts from carboxyl to amino group giving COO- and NH3+ - the zwitterion.
Groups run from non-polar aliphatic and aromatic through polar uncharged to positively and negatively charged.

worked_examples.q: How many standard amino acids enter proteins?

concepts.title: Peptide Bonds and Protein Structure Levels
concepts.definition: Coupling the carboxyl of one amino acid to the amino of the next forges a peptide bond with a water molecule lost at every link, so a chain of n residues holds n-1 such bonds; folding then stacks four levels - primary sequence, secondary alpha helix or beta sheet, tertiary packing with disulfide and hydrophobic ties, and quaternary assembly of subunits.
concepts.key_idea: One water leaves per bond, so subtract one from the residue count for bonds; multiply residues by 110 Da to size the protein.
question_patterns: how many peptide bonds form and how many water molecules are lost when eight amino acids join into an octapeptide
estimate the molecular weight of a polypeptide of 150 residues taking 110 Da per residue
name the four levels of protein structure and one stabilising force at each level
compare the hydrogen bonding pattern of an alpha helix with that of a beta pleated sheet
why cannot the peptide bond rotate freely - answer with its double bond character
what do the phi and psi angles specify and who proposed the plot that maps their allowed values
when do two identical subunits form a homodimer and what else can stabilise a quaternary structure

solution_steps.explain: A linear chain of n residues needs n-1 condensations.
Each condensation releases one water of 18 Da.
The mean residue mass is about 110 Da.

worked_examples.q: How many peptide bonds does a chain of 50 residues hold?

concepts.title: Nucleic Acids and the Double Helix
concepts.definition: Nucleotides - a nitrogenous base plus pentose sugar plus phosphate - string together through phosphodiester links into DNA or RNA; Watson and Crick wound two antiparallel strands into a right-handed double helix where adenine pairs thymine over two hydrogen bonds and guanine pairs cytosine over three, and heating melts the strands apart below-or-above a characteristic temperature until annealing re-pairs them.
concepts.key_idea: Two bonds per A-T pair and three per G-C pair let you total the hydrogen bonding holding any DNA segment together.
question_patterns: a 50 base pair segment holds 18 A-T pairs - how many hydrogen bonds knit the whole segment
why do G-C rich DNA stretches melt at a higher temperature than A-T rich ones
differentiate a nucleoside from a nucleotide with one example of each from DNA
list the differences between the sugar of DNA and that of RNA
compare A-DNA and Z-DNA with the standard B form on handedness and base pairs per helix
which bases absorb light near 260 nm and what does melting temperature mean
name the rRNA components of the 70S and the 80S ribosome and the arm of tRNA that carries the amino acid

solution_steps.explain: Subtract the A-T count from the total base pairs.
A-T pairs contribute two hydrogen bonds each and G-C pairs three.

worked_examples.q: How many hydrogen bonds join adenine to thymine?

worked_examples.source_ref: kebt103.txt section 3.4.1 (peptide bond water loss, 110 Da residue mass)
worked_examples.question_pattern: A polypeptide is assembled from {residues} amino acid residues. Find the number of peptide bonds formed, the total water lost, and the approximate molecular weight of the polypeptide.

extracted_variables.residues: number of amino acid residues joined

solution_template.explain: Each new residue adds exactly one peptide bond.
One water of 18 Da leaves per condensation.
Average residue mass is about 110 Da.

worked_examples.source_ref: kebt103.txt section 3.5 (A=T two bonds, G=C three bonds)
worked_examples.question_pattern: A double-stranded DNA segment of {bp_total} base pairs contains {at_pairs} A-T pairs. Find the number of G-C pairs and the total hydrogen bonds holding the segment together.

extracted_variables.bp_total: total base pairs in the segment

solution_template.explain: The rest of the segment must be G-C pairs.
Two per A-T pair, three per G-C pair.
